Yama
(‘one who controls’)
------------------------------------------
In the Ṛgveda, the word यम has been used in several mantras, in the sense of twins (vide 1.164.15; 2.39.2).
It has also been used to indicate a god or deity, sometimes identified with the Supreme (vide Ṛgveda 1.164.46).
As one of the deities like इन्द्र or वरुण, he is said to be the offspring of Vivasvān (the Sun) and his wife सṁज्ञा. Hence he is called वैवस्वत also. Yamī was his twin-sister.
He is the lord of the पितृस् or manes. He is the king of the पितृलोक, the world of the manes (ibid 9.113.8; 10.16.9).
It is he who is death for the human beings (ibid 10.165.4).
He sends the dead persons to the regions they deserve, good or bad (ibid 10.14.1).
The Kaṭha Upaniṣad is the teaching given by यम-वैवस्वत to the young seeker नचिकेतस्.
In the epics and the पुराणस् he is described as the lord of the South. His capital is the city called Saṁyamanī. Mahiṣa or the buffalo is his वाहन or mount. The river यमुना is his sister.
He gave many boons to अर्जुन when he was performing austerities at the Indrakīla mountain. He also gave many boons to सावित्री, being pleased with her devotion to her husband सत्यवान् (Mahābhārata, Vanaparva 297).
As a result of the curse of the sage अणिमाण्डव्य, यम was born as विदुर, considered a śūdra by caste (Mahābhārata, Ādiparva 108.16).
After testing Yudhiṣṭhira—his own spiritual son—as a यक्ष, he blessed him, fulfilling all his wishes (vide Vanaparva 313).
When he wanted to take away मार्कण्डेय after his life-duration was completed, he was chastised by Lord शिव.
It was he who reminded Rāma—at the end of his earthly sojourn—of his promise to return to वैकुण्ठ.
Yama is the first of the eight steps of योग. See YOGADARŚANA.

Yamaloka
(‘the world of यम’)
------------------------------------------
The Ṛgveda (10.135.1 and 7) gives a brief description of यमलोक or the world of यम as a wonderful place full of peace.
Yama lives there with his associates who praise him, to the accompaniment of मुसिच् of the flute.
According to the पुराणस् यमलोक is a vast place surrounded by four iron forts, with four main gates. There is a majestic auditorium wherein many great kings of the past assemble.
Naraka or हेल्ल् exists in one part of this world.
See also NARAKA and YAMA.

Yamagītā
(‘song of यम’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu epics and the पुराणस् contain a large number of religious discourses that often go by the name Gītā, obviously in imitation of the original, the Bhagavadgītā of the Mahābhārata.
There are three such pieces that are called Yamagītā. They are part of: the Viṣṇupurāṇa (3.7); the Agnipurāṇa (381); the Nṛsiṁhapurāṇa (8). Out of these, the one in the Viṣṇupurāṇa is more well-known. It has just 39 verses.
Maitreya asks पराशर about those karmas (actions, way of life) by which a person becomes free from the clutches of यम, the god of death. पराशर replies that नकुल had put the same question to भीष्म, the grandsire and that भीष्म had replied quoting a wise ब्राह्मण from the country of कलिङ्ग. This forms the content of the Yamagītā.
Once a dūta (servant) of यम who was to go out in search of the jīvas (souls of living beings) about to die, was advised by his master not to touch but leave off the devotees of विष्णु since he had no control over them. On being asked about the characteristics of a devotee of विष्णु, यम described them in detail as follows:
A devotee of विष्णु never transgresses the duties prescribed for his वर्ण and आश्रम. He is equanimous towards his friends and foes. He never harms others. He is ever pure in मिन्द् and always meditates upon विष्णु in his heart. He is free from the अरिषड्वर्ग (six passions like lust and greed). He is always peaceful both inside and outside. He can never commit sins or crimes.
Yama then narrated the signs of one who was not a devotee of Viṣṇu—an evil person. Such a person robs the wealth of others, tells lies and harms the living beings. He is arrogant, jealous and abuses others, especially the good ones. He never performs yajñas or sacrifices, does not give gifts to deserving persons, nor even treat his own kith and kin properly. Always being in the company of the evil ones, he is committing sins one after another.
Yama’s final words of advice to his servant were that he should never touch the devotees of विष्णु who were ever protected by his चक्र or the discus!

Yamunā
(‘that which rests [in the गङ्गा river after merging]’)
------------------------------------------
Yamunā (also spelt as Jamunā or Jumnā) is one of the most sacred rivers of India, next only to गङ्गा. It has been mentioned even in the Ṛgveda along with गङ्गा (vide 10.75.5). The king सुदास, with the help of the Tṛtsus, conquered the ten kings on the bank of the river यमुना (ibid 7.18.19). Kings भरत, अम्बरीष and Śantanu had performed several sacrifices on its banks. The great sage अगस्त्य had performed severe austerities on its bank.
In the epics and the पुराणस् it has been described as closely connected with the boyhood days of Lord कृष्ण, like the Rāsalīlā (See RĀSALĪLĀ.). When Vasudeva (Kṛṣṇa’s ड़थेर्) carried baby कृष्ण, यमुना is said to have split into two giving way, to facilitate his going.
The river takes its birth in Yamunotrī in the Kalinda mountain, a part of the Himālayan range (Hence it got the name कालिन्दी.). After coursing through 1376 kilometres (854 miles) it joins the गङ्गा and the invisible सरस्वती at the त्रिवेणी-saṅgam of प्रयाग (the modern Allahabad).
The Māghamelā bathing festival that is held here every year as also the कुम्भमेला held once in 12 years (during January-February), attracts millions of devotees.
The river has several other names such as Sūryatanayā and Śamanasvasā.
The quantity of water and the flow of the river are more or less constant through out the year. Several tributaries, melting of Himālayan icebergs in summer and greater in-flow during the rainy season seem to be the reason behind it.
Since the river often breaks into smaller streams which join it later, several small islands are formed in it.
Delhi, the old part of the capital city, is situated on its banks. वृन्दाबन् and मथुरा, the famous places of pilgrimage—because of their association with Kṛṣṇa—are also on its banks. Rājāpur, the birthplace of Tulasīdās (A.

-1623) is also situated on its bank.
Waters of यमुना appear rather black or dark in colour because शिव, overcome by the intense sorrow over the loss of his wife सती, is said to have jumped into this river once!
Yamunā is also the goddess or the presiding deity of the river. She was the daughter of सूर्य (the Sun-god) and Saṁjñādevī. यम, the god of death was her twin-brother. She is said to have invited her brother यम to her होउसे on the Kārttika-śukla-dvitīyā day (during the दीपावली festival, usually in November) and honoured him with dinner and presents. This day is known as यम-dvitīyā or Bhrātṛdvitīyā. On this day sisters invite their brothers for sumptuous meals and exchange presents. (Hence a bath in the यमुना river on this day is considered extremely auspicious.)
Iconographic works describe her as black in colour, standing upon a black tortoise (kṛṣṇakacchapa) and wearing a garland of blue lotuses. She has two arms, the hands showing the varada and the abhaya mudrās (gestures of boon-giving and protection). Her sculptured images are seen in the Udayagiri caves near Bhuvaneśvar in Orissa as also the museum at Patna in Bihar.
Like गङ्गा, यमुना also has been praised profusely as मोथेर् in the devotional songs composed by saints.
See also GAṄGĀ.

------------------------------------------
The foundation of the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta philosophy, of which Rāmānujā-cārya (A.
-1137) was the chief exponent, was laid by a succession of ten ācāryas or teachers before him. Of them नाथमुनि (A.

-924) and Yāmuna or यामुनाचार्य were the most prominent ones.
यामुनाचार्य">Idol of YāmunācāryaYāmuna—also known as Āḷavandār—was born in A.

as the son of Īśvaramuni, the son of नाथमुनि. Vīranārāyaṇapura (in Tamil Nadu) was the place where he lived. At the tender age of twelve he is said to have conquered (in disputation) a great scholar Akki Āḷvār. Consequently the Coḷa king, being immensely pleased with him, gave him half the kingdom. He lived as a king enjoying all the good things of life. However, at the age of 80 he took सṁन्यास and settled down at श्रीरङ्गम्, the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे with its temple of रङ्गनाथ.
He worked hard to make the temple of श्रीरङ्गम् the central place of श्रीवैष्णविस्म्. (See SRĪVAIṢṆAVISM.)
Though he had a great desire to make Rāmānuja his disciple, to succeed him to the pontifical seat he was occupying, he passed away before he could do so.
He had 21 disciples of whom the following five were the chief ones: Mahāpūrṇa, Śrīśailapūrṇa, गोष्ठीपूर्ण, Mālādhara and Vararaṅganāyaka.
He wrote six works: Stotraratna; Catuśślokī; Āgamaprāmāṇya; Siddhitraya; गीतार्थसङ्ग्रह; Mahāpuruṣanirṇaya.
The first is a beautiful hymn on नारायण. The second praises the role of his spouse लक्ष्मी in granting लिबेरतिओन् to the jīvas (the individual souls). In the third he proves that the Pāñcarātra Āgamas are as authoritative as the वेदस्.
The Siddhitraya is his chief work on the philosophy of Viśiṣṭhādvaita, wherein he has tried to prove that ब्रह्मन् and जीव are separate entities, the relation between them being one of शेष (part) and śeṣin (whole).
In the Gītārthasaṅgraha he has shown that it is नारायण-Parabrahma that is attained through the three disciplines of कर्म (action), ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion). It is भक्ति that is the chief means.
In the last work—the Mahāpuruṣa-nirṇaya—he has tried to establish that the God described in the उपनिषद्स् and the पुराणस् is नारायण.

Yamasmṛti
------------------------------------------
Many writers of धर्मशास्त्रस् have quoted several verses from यम or Yamasmṛti on various topics. Though no authentic work of that title has been recovered, it is possible that a fairly big work of that name existed. There are some printed editions published by various agencies, but the number of verses is different from one another, like 78 or 99 or 182. Some treatises called Bṛhad-Yama are also available in print.
The topics dealt with in these printed editions are: प्रायश्चित्त (expiation for sins); शुद्धि (purification); śrāddha (obsequial rites); lowest castes; पर्तितिओन्; ड़ोओद् and its pollution; च्रिमे अन्द् पुनिस्ह्मेन्त्; litigation; some philosophical topics.
Many of the verses quoted by the authors of the धर्मशास्त्रस् are usually found in the printed edition of Manusmṛti.

Yamasūkta
------------------------------------------
The Yamasūkta is a part of the Ṛgveda (10.14). It comprises 16 ṛks or mantras. यम, the god of death and धर्म (righteousness), is the ṛṣi or the sage to whom it was revealed. यम, the पितृस् (manes) and Sārameyas (the two fierce dogs of यम) are the देवतास् (divinities) to whom the सूक्त is addressed.
The first मन्त्र urges the yajamāna (the sacrificer) to worship (with oblations) यम, who takes the souls of beings who have performed good deeds, to higher worlds safely.
The second मन्त्र praises यम because he knows the paths by which he takes us all.
The third मन्त्र declares that the gods like इन्द्र, यम and बृहस्पति are mutually benefited by the offerings given with the formulas—svadhā and svāhā—by the पितृस् like Aṅgirasas and Ṛkvis.
The fourth मन्त्र invites यम to come along with the पितृस् called Aṅgirās and make the sacrificer happy.
In the fifth मन्त्र, Vivasvān (the ड़थेर् of यम) is also invited for the same purpose.
After declaring that the pitṛs—the Atharvas, the Bhṛgus and the Navagvas—are worthy of worship with the offerings of the सोम juice, the sixth मन्त्र expresses the wish that we may deserve to receive their grace and blessing.
If a yajamāna dies before the sacrifice is completed, the होतृ (priest of the Ṛgveda) recites the seventh and the eighth mantras wherein the प्रेत (the spirit) of the dead person is advised to travel by the ‘ancient path’ and meet यम as also वरुण.
The ninth मन्त्र commands the evil spirits in the च्रेमतिओन् ground to depart immediately since यम has allotted this place to the dead person.
The tenth मन्त्र exhorts the spirit of the dead person to travel safely, avoiding the two fierce dogs of यम (Sārameyas).
At the same time, prayer is offered to यम, in the eleventh मन्त्र, to see that his dogs protect this spirit.
The twelfth मन्त्र describes how the two dogs of यम move about in this world, among persons who are about to die, to take them to यम.
In the thirteenth मन्त्र, there is an appeal or a direction to the ṛtviks (concerned priests) to press the सोम juice to be offered to यम.
In the fourteenth, the ṛtviks are requested to offer the oblation of ghee to यम so that he can grant a long life.
In the next, the fifteenth, मन्त्र there is, once more, an appeal to the ṛtviks to give sweet oblations of पुरोडाश to यम. Then obeisance is offered to the ancient ṛṣis.
The last मन्त्र, the sixteenth, describes यम as taking part in three kinds of sacrifice—Jyotiḥ, Gauḥ and Āyuḥ—and also occupying six regions of च्रेअतिओन् to witness the doings of all living beings. Some of these mantras are used in aparakarmas or the rites performed after the death of a person.
